description: I am a Space Science undergraduate at the University of the Punjab with interests in GIS, Remote Sensing, Earth Observation, GeoAI, and space technology. I have experience with QGIS, ArcGIS, Google Earth Engine, and basic Python. I enjoy research, problem-solving, and developing innovative solutions to real-world challenges. I welcome passionate teammates with skills in programming, AI/ML, data science, web development, and scientific research who are eager to collaborate.
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a storytelling project that explores the forgotten legacy of NASA's discarded and inactive equipment on the Moon and Mars. Through engaging visual storytelling, historical research, and space exploration facts, we highlight the landers, rovers, scientific instruments, and other human-made objects that remain on these celestial bodies long after their missions have ended.

Our project brings attention to the stories behind these machines: why they were sent, what scientific discoveries they made, how they contributed to our understanding of space, and why they were eventually left behind. By transforming technical mission histories into an accessible and compelling narrative, we aim to connect audiences with the human achievements and challenges of planetary exploration.

This project is important because these forgotten machines are more than abandoned equipment; they represent scientific progress, innovation, and humanity's first steps toward exploring other worlds. Their stories deserve to be remembered as part of our continuing journey into space.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?
Our project tells the stories of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, written for school-age space fans. A seven-slide storytelling deck follows each machine’s journey: the Lunar Roving Vehicles of Apollo 15, 16 and 17, the laser reflectors of Apollo 11, 14 and 15, the Mars rovers Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, the helicopter Ingenuity, and the probes Voyager 1, Voyager 2 and Pioneer 10. Each machine gets the same layout: launch or landing date and place, a big number (distance driven, years of work, or year of last contact), and a one-line fate. A companion cinematic film is an auto-playing web page with animated space backdrops, captions and optional voice narration.

What benefits does it have?
The cards are simple and consistent, so a young reader can compare machines at a glance. The story goes from the Moon to Mars to deep space, ending on the idea that these machines are abandoned but not forgotten. The “still working” examples, the Apollo laser reflectors and the Voyagers, show kids that old hardware can still produce science.

What is the intended impact?
We want young people to see these machines as characters with journeys, and to get curious about the missions and the open NASA data behind them. A forgotten machine stays forgotten only until someone tells its story.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG for the illustrations.
  • A canvas starfield, CSS animation, and the browser’s built-in speech feature for narration.
  • Google Fonts: Space Grotesk and Inter.
  • Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) helped us draft the slide text and build the deck and film page.
  • Our facts come from NASA mission pages and the NSSDCA catalog.

How is your project creative?

  • Every machine is told as a short journey with an ending, not as a list of specifications.
  • The same story is told twice: once as slides to present, and once as a film-style page with moving backdrops and narration.
  • Colours and backgrounds change from scene to scene: grey lunar ground, rust-red Mars, a purple-blue nebula in deep space.
  • It uses the “still working” twist, with the reflectors and Voyagers showing that abandoned does not mean useless.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: school-age readers, so plain wording and big numbers.
  • Accuracy: dates, distances and counts come from NASA sources, and approximate figures are marked with “~”. The reflectors are shown on the Moon, not in deep space.
  • Clarity: at most seven slides, one idea per slide, and readable text sizes.
  • Access: captions on the film, and a voice option that can be turned off.
